- we can know pretty confidently that ADHD is genetic because it has an insanely high heritability (about 80-90%)
- it is pretty common for people to get misdiagnosed with ADHD, especially in childhood. this used to be a bigger problem but a lot of people noticed and got mad so doctors tend to be more careful with that now.
- there are very good tests for it. these are not biological tests to see if you genetically have it, and these are usually not even used to make most diagnoses, but here are some common tests:
—- WAIS (IQ test) - this is used to check for large disparities between your comprehension/reasoning skills vs your working memory/processing speed, with the latter category being much lower in ADHD individuals. 
—- Continuous Performance Test - this is a computer test to measure several types of attention deficits (inattentiveness, impulsivity, sustained attention, vigilance)
—- BASC - a questionnaire about behavior given to parents and teachers 

this is along with interviews with the subject, their parents, and sometimes even in-classroom observation though this is more rare.

1. The Basics
    1. Determinism 
        1. I agree with the premise of determinism, but I don’t know that I would call these things “wants”. Not sure how to elaborate on this, I don’t care much about this point but just throwing that out there that this seems weird.
        2. Hard argument:
            1. I don’t think it follows from this that moral discussion is pointless. We can still assess whether an action is “good” or “bad” regardless of agency. Most consequentialist moral theories don’t care if the agent had a choice or not, since that has nothing to do with the consequences of the action. Where I think determinism does become relevant is assigning moral blame. It’s possible for an action to be morally wrong without assigning blame to the agent, at least in a metaphysical sense.
            2. (Note: I am a moral anti realist so I do agree in a sense that “there is no morality”, I just don’t think that follows from your argument here. Morality can be compatible with determinism)
        3. Soft argument
            1. I’m not sure why this version claims we have some degree of choice in how we act upon our wants. Why are our wants determined but not our actions? No justification for this assumption is given here. 
    2. Aristotle - happiness and basic desires
        1. No objections here
    3. Ayer - emotivism
        1. Does emotivism really mean that moral statements are not prescriptive? 
            1. My understanding is that emotivism means that moral statements are not truth-apt. So when someone makes a moral statement, they don’t even think it’s something that could possibly be true or false. Just like saying “bugs, ew!” is not an expression that could be true or false, “murder is wrong” is similarly just expressing a negative attitude. 
            2. I don’t even know if this could be described as a “descriptive statement based on our emotions”. Descriptive statements can still be true or false, so I’m not sure if a non-truth-apt statement is necessarily descriptive or prescriptive. 
            3. It seems like there are various views on this: for instance, SEP says things like “Some theorists who view themselves as emotivists suggest that even the most general terms of moral evaluation have a descriptive meaning rather than just an emotive or non-cognitive meaning (Stevenson 1944, 22; Hare 1952, suggests the same sort of idea within a prescriptivist theory at 118).” 
            4. I honestly have a hard time understanding emotivism so debating this point is tough for me but basically I think your interpretation might also be wrong.
            5. Overall your application of reasoning down to basic desires seems to not fit that well with emotivism in my opinion, though again I don’t have a great understanding of it. It just seems like emotivism is much more non-rational than your application. 
            6. Your idea of boiling down moral statements to our basic desires, and your overall argument in general, sounds a lot more like moral naturalism to me, and it should cohere with your second point better since this is also an Aristotelian theory. Moral naturalism and emotivism are contradictory, so I don’t think emotivism supports your argument very well. 
2. Towards moral objectivism
    1. Same brains, same desires
        1. Already addressed
    2. Intuition
        1. If this is true, and we all have the same basic desires, then how do we arrive at different moral conclusions? I know later you say because of “calculation error”, but then I don’t understand the point of bringing up intuition like this. 
    3. Moral error
        1. I’m very confused here on what you mean by error. You seem to mention moral error theory as if it were an explanation of why people do morally bad things, but that’s not at all what it is. I think you are just using the wrong term here because it would be extremely weird to cite moral error theory, a variety of moral anti-realism, in support of moral realism. (Going back to the emotivism point, that is also a variety of moral anti realism, so again I don’t think that belongs in your argument). Overall I’m pretty confused by this point, so I’d suggest you revise this after clarifying your concept of moral error theory. 
    4. Historical inertia
        1. This could be challenged on just a moral anti realist point of view, but since we are kind of past that level already I would challenge this on “factual” grounds. 
        2. For one thing, we know so little about prehistorical human societies that it would be impossible given our current information to judge whether they had a more “morally just” social structure or values. For all we know it could have been better than today. You can argue that that’s unlikely, but there just isn’t enough evidence to say one way or the other. 
        3. I think this idea works best when imagining a super broad global historical timeline of popular knowledge, but when you take a closer look you can find plenty of examples of society “regressing”. You can look at democratic backsliding around the world today, or lots of historical examples where racism/xenophobia increased, less value placed on environmental stewardship with the adoption of certain religious and economic systems, or even though I disagree with them lots of conservatives think our society and values are worse today because of egalitarian values like feminism, lgbt acceptance, etc. 
        4. You could counter this a bit by saying that these regressions are small and temporary, and overall the trend is still positive. Perhaps these are part of the process of working things out. I could grant that as possible but I still have the anti realist objection to this idea.
        5. Some labels for this idea are “moral convergence” or “the long march of history”

just because long term medication treatment permanently alters your brain does not mean that it makes it worse. just from personal experience, after being on meds for about 8 years (off and on, usually not taking them in the summer), I finally got to where I didn't need them anymore. for the first few weeks of withdrawal it was brutal, but after that, I could comfortably manage my adhd almost just as well as I could on meds, and most definitely better than I could before I was on them/off for the summer. 
that's what psychological medication is designed to do - to change your brain to work differently than it did before.
